sources.news_title: Kohberger seeks to challenge conviction for murders of Idaho college students
sources.text:
Bryan Kohberger trying to challenge conviction for University of Idaho murders, documents say
Bryan Kohberger, who pleaded guilty last year for fatally stabbing four University of Idaho students, is seeking to challenge his conviction, according to new court documents.
Kohberger said he filed a petition to reopen the case and that he blamed his plea on “false promises” and wrong information.
A post conviction relief form was filed Monday in Idaho, court filings show. Kohberger also confirmed his efforts in a statement sent from prison to The New York Times.
"My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn," part of his statement said.
Ethan Chapin, 20; Kaylee Goncalves, 21; Xana Kernodle, 20; and Madison Mogen, 21, were fatally stabbed in the early morning hours of November 13, 2022, in Moscow, Idaho, authorities said.
Kohberger was convicted last July after entering a guilty plea, during which he publicly admitted to the four killings for the first time.
In a stunning hearing a year ago, Kohberger admitted to killing the students.
“Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?” Judge Steven Hippler asked at the time.
“Yes,” Kohberger replied.
He was then sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
As part of his plea, Kohberger waived the right to appeal, but that does not preclude him from filing a new case challenging the validity of his plea agreement.
In a statement provided to ABC News, the family of Goncalves said Kohberger "chose not to leave his fate — or the facts of the case — to a jury."
"We would have preferred a death-penalty trial; we believe fully in the evidence," the family said. "Instead, [Kohberger] received exactly what he asked for: a deal that spared his life. Know this — he hates that life. He wants another chance to roll the dice."
The family statement also says a day in court, if granted, would allow Kohberger to have a "welcome break from solitary confinement: a ride, perhaps different food, photos taken, and the spotlight once again fixed on him and his supposed 'innocence.'"
The office of Anne Taylor, one of Kohberger’s attorneys, declined to comment.
The Latah County Prosecutor’s Office is also not commenting citing “pending litigation.”
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said in a statement to CNN that his office is “ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out.”
“My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news,” the statement read.
Kohberger, a PhD student of criminology at nearby Washington State University, was charged with killing the four students in January 2023.
He was arrested in Pennsylvania more than a month after the stabbings in the small college town shocked the nation. Forensic DNA testing from trash collected outside his family’s home gave Idaho law enforcement the probable cause to take him into custody.
Prosecutors had submitted a variety of evidence they say tied Kohberger to the crimes, including DNA found on a knife sheath on a bed close to Mogen. The single source profile was determined to be male and detectives matched it to Kohberger through investigative genetic genealogy.
As they prepared for trial, Kohberger’s defense attorneys said he was out driving alone on the night of the killings.
The case was delayed numerous times, including by a change of venue, frustrating the victims’ families. After previously pleading not guilty, Kohberger agreed to enter a plea deal to avoid the death penalty.

sources.text:
Bryan Kohberger, the man convicted of killing four University of Idaho students in 2022, is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and wants his day in court.
Kohberger, who pleaded guilty in July 2025 to avoid a quadruple murder trial and is serving four life sentences, filed a “petition for post conviction relief” Monday in the Ada County District Court in Idaho.
A petition for post-conviction relief is a way to challenge a conviction outside the appeals process. The court record indicates that Kohberger is representing himself.
It was not immediately clear on what grounds he was seeking the petition.
But in an interview with The New York Times, Kohberger claimed he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the murders.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” he said in a statement to the newspaper Sunday night.
Dismissing the state investigators’ account of what happened as a “myopic narrative” and a “work of fiction,” Kohberger said in the statement that “its faulty premises were never challenged at trial.”
“Circumnavigated by a broken plea, the trial never provided the public the clarity conducive to closure, and justice shall remain abjectly miscarried unless that plea is withdrawn,” the statement said.
Kohberger admitted last year to killing the four students — Madison Mogen, 21; Kaylee Goncalves, 21; Xana Kernodle, 20; and Ethan Chapin, 20 — at an off-campus house on Nov. 13, 2022.
A doctoral student in criminal justice at the time of the murders, Kohberger took a plea deal and was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences for four counts of first-degree murder and 10 years in prison for a burglary charge.
While he told a judge that he broke into the off-campus house in Moscow, Idaho, and killed four of the six students there, most of them as they slept, he has never said what motivated the killings.
Before the filing, Kohberger had not made any public statements suggesting he might change his plea.
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said his office “stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out.”
“My heart goes out to the families of Madison, Kaylee, Xana, and Ethan, who have already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today’s deeply painful news,” he posted on X.
The Goncalves family referred to Kohberger in a statement as “the mosquito you just can’t seem to swat” and criticized The New York Times for providing him with a platform.
“The piece had little else to offer beyond a guilty man once again claiming he is innocent,” it said.
The Goncalves family said they wanted Kohberger to face trial — and a possible death penalty. But Kohberger opted to plead guilty.
“He wants another chance to roll the dice,” the family said in the statement. “The defendant will get another day in court—a welcome break from solitary confinement: a ride, perhaps different food, photos taken, and the spotlight once again fixed on him and his supposed ‘innocence’.”

sources.text:
Man convicted in Idaho college killings seeks to take back guilty plea
The criminology student convicted last year of murdering four University of Idaho students in their home is seeking to abandon his guilty plea and obtain a trial, claiming he is innocent and was misled into confessing to the high-profile killings.
In an interview with The New York Times, Bryan Kohberger, who is serving four life sentences, said he had filed a petition challenging his conviction, citing concerns about how the plea deal came together.
“My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn,” Kohberger said in a statement provided to the Times on Sunday night. He reiterated in a phone call from prison in Idaho that he had an “absolute claim of innocence.”
Kohberger had not granted an interview or made public comments before speaking with the Times. He declined to discuss any evidence or other specific details related to his innocence claim, as well as what specific concerns he had about the plea process.
It is rare for defendants to win post-conviction challenges, which often revolve around claims of newly discovered evidence or an ineffective assistance of counsel.
Steve Goncalves, the father of one of the victims, declined to comment this morning, saying he wanted to discuss the issue with his family. The Latah County Prosecutor’s Office did not immediately return a call seeking comment.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
In November 2022, the four murders in Moscow, Idaho, a college town that had not seen a homicide in seven years, captivated the country for weeks as investigators struggled to identify a suspect. Kohberger’s arrest brought relief to the community but also stoked further mystery and speculation, as investigators never identified a motive or any previous relationship with the victims.
In court, law enforcement officials outlined the evidence against Kohberger. His DNA was found on a Ka-Bar knife sheath that had been left next to two of the victims. Amazon records showed he had purchased a Ka-Bar knife and sheath months prior. He drove a white Elantra, the type of car that investigators determined had been on surveillance video circling the crime scene and then speeding away from it. Kohberger’s phone showed he was out that night, with his phone turned off at the time of the murders.
Kohberger declined to discuss the evidence against him in his call with the Times. He said, “The intention is for all of those questions to be investigated and answered appropriately in a trial setting.”
Kohberger, who had court-appointed representation throughout the case, ending with his guilty plea, said he prepared the documentation to challenge the case on his own. He will seek to have a lawyer appointed to help him going forward. Records show the filing reached the court this morning.
After he was arrested in December 2022, Kohberger’s initial lawyer said his client was eager to be exonerated. Court-appointed lawyers spent more than two years challenging the evidence collected against Kohberger, only for a surprise plea deal to come together a few weeks before a trial was to begin.
Kohberger accepted responsibility for the murders at a July 2025 hearing. He was not required to offer a motive for the killings — and never has. The lack of a detailed confession outraged some of the victims’ family members and even President Donald Trump, who had called on the judge to demand an explanation from Kohberger.
In court, the judge asked Kohberger, “Are you pleading guilty because you are guilty?”
“Yes,” Kohberger responded. He later sat in silence at a sentencing hearing at which family members of the victims expressed their grief and anger.
In the early morning hours of Nov. 13, 2022, after a typical Saturday night out, the four victims were stabbed to death in an off-campus home. The bodies of Madison Mogen, 21, and Kaylee Goncalves, 21, were found together in a bed on the home’s third floor. The bodies of Xana Kernodle, 20, and her boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, 20, were found in a bedroom on the second floor.
Two surviving roommates were in a bedroom on the home’s first floor. One of them reported seeing a shadowy figure in the middle of the night and hearing a commotion. But the roommates did not seek help until later in the morning, saying they had not realized what had transpired.
One of the experts who worked on Kohberger’s defense team has taken particular issue with the plea arrangement and the evidence. Brent Turvey, a forensic scientist who analyzed the crime scene for the defense, argued that the crime was committed by multiple perpetrators, criticized how investigators documented evidence and questioned why more testing was not done of a hair found with one of the victims.
The lawyers who served as Kohberger’s defense team have rebuked Turvey, telling The Idaho Statesman that he “is now speaking about topics that are still confidential, many of which are outside of his areas of expertise.” The lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday. Turvey’s concerns were included in a book about the case, “Broken Plea.”
Kohberger alluded to those issues in his statement, saying that “unanswered questions seem to multiply with each piece of discovery unsealed.” He said he was not concerned that, if offered a new trial, he could face the death penalty.
“Why am I breaking my silence?” Kohberger said Sunday in the interview from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution, just south of Boise. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.”
Kohberger grew up in Pennsylvania and moved to Pullman, Washington, in 2022 to pursue a doctorate in the criminal justice and criminology program at Washington State University, just across the state border from the University of Idaho. He had long been interested in serial killers and the minds of criminals.
Kohberger had signed a plea agreement agreeing that he “knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waives all rights to appeal any and all issues in this case.” Still, defendants can make other claims about the legal process through post-conviction relief.

sources.text:
The man sentenced to serve four consecutive terms of life in prison for the killing of four University of Idaho students wants to take back his guilty plea.
Bryan Kohberger told the New York Times that he was misled and offered "false promises" before agreeing to plead guilty to the killings of Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin and Xana Kernodle.
The New York Times said Kohberger told them of his efforts over the phone and provided a statement that he has an "absolutely claim of innocence."
"My actual innocence is my truth, and the plea, hinged on by false promises and blatant disinformation, MUST be withdrawn," Kohberger said in a statement.
Kohberger spoke by phone from the maximum-security prison in Kuna, Idaho where he has been serving his prison sentences, representing the first time he had done so with the media since he was arrested.
A petition filed in Ada County Court on Monday confirmed Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea and expanded on his reasoning. Kohberger argued that he was convinced by his counsel that actual guilt wasn't relevant to his plea and that his guilty plea was necessary to avoid the death penalty. He also argued that his attorneys ignored exculpatory evidence.
Kohberger pleaded guilty to the killings in July of 2025, more than two years after the killings. His guilty plea and the terms of his agreement with prosecutors were considered in a public hearing by Ada County Judge Steven Hippler. Hippler signed off on the agreement after Kohberger confirmed that he was guilty of the crime and that he was properly represented.
Those statements by Kohberger after his attorneys reached the agreement with prosecutors pose an obstacle for his new efforts to retract his plea, but a reversal is possible if he can prove he was improperly represented or present new evidence.
A reversal of his guilty plea wouldn't guarantee him a better outcome. At the time when his plea agreement was announced, members of at least one of the families of the victims were outraged that the Latah County Prosecutor's Office accepted the deal that took the death penalty off the table.

What The Law Says
The legal mechanisms governing guilty pleas in Idaho depend heavily on timing. Under Idaho Rule of Criminal Procedure 33(c), requests made prior to sentencing are evaluated under a relatively lenient standard that allows withdrawal for any fair and just reason. Once a judge has formally imposed a sentence, however, the standard shifts dramatically. Post-sentencing withdrawals are permitted only to correct a manifest injustice. Because Kohberger has already been sentenced, his legal team must convince the court that leaving his original conviction intact would result in a clear, fundamental miscarriage of justice.
Proving a manifest injustice requires meeting a high evidentiary bar. Courts typically consider a plea vulnerable only if the defendant can show that it was entered involuntarily, that defense counsel provided constitutionally ineffective assistance, or that prosecutorial misconduct prejudiced the outcome. While Kohberger's public statement claims he was misled by false promises and disinformation, he previously affirmed under oath during his change-of-plea hearing before Judge Steven Hippler that he understood the agreement, was acting voluntarily, and was entering the plea because he was in fact guilty. Overcoming those sworn statements in open court will require substantial, concrete evidence rather than broad assertions.
Complicating matters further is the legal framework surrounding post-conviction appeals. As part of his original plea agreement, Kohberger formally waived his right to a direct appeal. While such waivers do not entirely bar post-conviction petitions based on severe constitutional violations or newly discovered evidence, courts view post-sentence retractions with profound skepticism. Unless his defense team can present tangible proof of coercion, fraud, or egregious errors that directly corrupted the plea process, legal observers emphasize that courts rarely overturn a settled guilty plea at this stage.
The Idaho Post-Conviction Procedure Act Explained
In Idaho, once a criminal defendant has been sentenced and exhausted or waived their direct appeal rights, the primary legal avenue to challenge a conviction is through the Uniform Post-Conviction Procedure Act (Idaho Code § 19-4901 et seq.). Unlike a direct appeal—which only reviews the existing record for legal errors made by the judge—a post-conviction petition initiates a separate, civil proceeding. This framework allows a defendant to introduce new evidence or raise constitutional claims that were not fully developed on the record during the original plea or trial proceedings.
Because a post-conviction petition is legally classified as a civil action, the burden of proof rests entirely on the petitioner to establish their claims by a preponderance of the evidence. Common grounds for relief under the Act include substantial constitutional violations, such as ineffective assistance of counsel, coerced guilty pleas, or prosecutorial misconduct, as well as newly discovered evidence that could not have been uncovered before sentencing through due diligence. “Why am I breaking my silence?” Kohberger remarked from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution. “A lot went wrong in those plea discussions. I really do want that to be heard.”

KAYLEE Goncalves and Madison Mogen were inseparable. Best friends since childhood, they did everything together – even attending the same university in Idaho.
When they shared an apartment off campus with three other girls – and Xana Kernodle – they felt like soul mates.
Bryan Kohberger has never given any reason why he carried out such atrocious murders Credit: Getty Victims Madison Mogen, 21, and Kaylee Goncalves, 21, who were killed in their off-campus home Credit: AlamyXana’s likeable boyfriend and fellow student, Ethan Chapin, was also there for much of the time and they would all socialise together.
It was known as a fun, party house, where people would come and go, when not studying. But their dreams for the future were brutally ended for four of them in the early hours of the morning of 13 November 2022 when an intruder entered and before making his escape.
The incident shocked the community, the country and the world as word spread about this night of horror.
Four years on, the harrowing Sky documentary, The Idaho Murders, features extensive police bodycam footage at , new insights and the lasting impact on the wider community in this quiet college town of Moscow in .
Ethan Chapin and Xana Kernodle, a young couple whose lives were also brutally cut short Credit: Instagram The Steptoe Village at Washington State University, where Bryan Christopher Kohberger, the graduate student at the school accused of first-degree murder in the stabbing deaths of four University of Idaho students, rented an apartment Credit: Reuters Ka-Bar similar to the weapon which the killer used in 2022 Credit: Rich Bowen/CC BY 2.0 Cops released photos of the crime scene, including a photo of two handprints on the window Credit: Moscow Police Department“They’ve demolished the house in King Road, where it happened,” says former student at the University of Idaho, Taylor Dolezal.
“The owner of the house gave it to the university and the university decided, ‘We are tearing it down. We’re just going to demolish it. It really helped with the closure of this case.
“Moscow will always be changed because of this. I think, ultimately, the spirit of the university, the fact that it is a college town, means it will bounce back. But there will always be kind of a heaviness surrounding the place, unfortunately.”
On the day before the murders, the local football team had a match. As usual on such Saturdays, there was drinking and socialising by excited fans, before and after the game.
An ominous fog swept in early evening and the temperature dropped. After the football had ended, the five friends made plans to go out.
Bethany and Dylan went home to 1122 King Road earlier than the others and went to bed. and Madison returned together in the early hours, as did Xana and Ethan.
The last one to bed was Xana, who had ordered a food delivery that arrived around 4am.
Tragically, there was another arrival – a tall, slim man dressed in black with a balaclava that just showed his eyes and “bushy eyebrows” as Dylan recalled.
A tired Dylan was awoken several times during the night – first by Kaylee’s dog, whining, then somebody crying and later thumping and a female saying “I think someone’s here.”
Then she heard a male voice say, “It’s okay. I’m going to help you.”
Thinking that it was one of the other girl’s boyfriends staying over, she went back to bed until she was awoken by more moving around. When she opened her door to look out, she was terrified to see a man in black walking towards her.
She shut her door, frozen in fear, locked it and heard him leave out of the glass, sliding door, in the kitchen.
Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed in Kohberger’s rampage Credit: Instagram/kayleegoncalves Cara Northington, mother of victim Xana Kernodle, wipes a tear at the sentencing hearing of Bryan Kohberger Credit: APCalling her roommates, she got no answer but met up with Bethany downstairs.
After finding Xana lying on the floor, the girls made a panicky emergency call, saying: “Something’s happened in our house and we don’t know what. One of the roommates is passed out. She was drunk last night and she’s not waking up. And they saw some man in the house last night.”
Police arrived and saw blood soaking into the carpets and mattresses and splattered on the walls.
Anthony Dahlinger, Chief of Police, Moscow Police Department, recalls, “It was an horrific scene. Something I will never forget.”
Kaylee and Madison had been repeatedly stabbed to death as they slept in the same bed together. Ethan was in bed, with his jugular slit.
Xana had begun to eat her food when she had been disturbed by the intruder. She had been stabbed over 50 times, with lots of defensive wounds, indicating that there had been a struggle.
“They were just young college kids, going to school to get an education and go out and enjoy their lives,” says Anthony.
“There was nothing obvious as to why someone would want to harm them.”
While survivors, Bethany and Dylan sat outside the house with some friends, police searched the house. At this stage, they did not know that their housemates were dead.
It was only when their university sent a text alert to all students that police were on site investigating a quadruple homicide that they knew.
Devastated Benjamin Mogen (R), father of Madison Mogen, cries at the court Credit: EPA Dylan Mortensen survived the horrific ordeal Credit: EPAThe documentary shows them at the moment of receiving the text, crying in horror and disbelief.
With the killer still on the loose and the police with no idea who it was, fear rapidly spread throughout the town. Would the attacker strike again?
“We all felt incredibly heartbroken and scared and we wanted to make some sense of how something like this could happen,” says Taylor Dolezal.
“It was inconceivable. We were terrified that there were going to be more. That it wouldn’t stop at the four.”

Desperate to find the murderer as quick as possible, fearing he might strike again, Moscow Police got the and state police involved.
They were jubilant when the sheath was found to have single male on it. Another vital discovery was CCTV footage of a car, identified as a white Hyundai Elantra, making multiple passes around the house for almost an hour on the day of the murders.

at speed, out of the neighbourhood and almost hit a rubbish bin on the side of the road.
There was no match of the DNA on the databases but experts in DNA genealogy were able to create a genome, identifying that it had above 80 per cent of Italian lineage.
They began to build a family tree until they found one couple whose child
was likely to be the person with the DNA found on the sheath. That couple only had one child – a son, named .
He was 28, from Pennsylvania, and a graduate student at Washington State University, studying criminology. He owned a white Hyundai Elantra and lived in student housing at WSU, in the Pullman area.
Gary Jenkins, former chief of WSU Police Department, was asked to meet with the Moscow Police Department.
“They said, ‘We have a suspect who is a graduate student at Washington State University and his name is Bryan Kohberger,” he says.
“When they told me the name, it rang a bell but I didn’t immediately know why. It took me thirty seconds or so and then I said, ‘I’ve talked to Bryan Kohberger before. I interviewed him for a research assistant position at Pullman Police Department in April. I have his resume and his cover letter.’ Their ears pricked up.
“When I interviewed him, he was kind of an odd guy. Not enough to raise a red flag that he would go out and do something horrible. But his personality was a little bit off. I thought that he probably couldn’t relate well to people and I didn’t select him.”
During the course of their investigation into Kohberger, it became apparent that on 14 October 2022 – one month before the murders – a cop had pulled him over in his car for jumping a red light.
Bodycam footage of their conversation is shown in the documentary, revealing Kohberger’s, long, gaunt face and scary, bulging eyes.
A month after the murders, he was stopped again by traffic cops. This time on his way to his parents’ house in Pennsylvania, to spend the break there, accompanied by his father in the passenger seat.
This time, the offence was for driving too closely to the vehicle in front.
Police bodycam of this, too, was captured. Six weeks after the murders, police went to his parent’s house in Albrightsville, Pennsylvania, almost 3,000 miles away from Moscow, where they saw the white Hyundai Elantra.
It had almost been taken apart inside and had been scrubbed to
get rid of DNA. Police grabbed a rubbish bag from the kerb outside the house. Inside, they found a Q-tip which had some ear wax on it.
This provided them with a DNA sample which, one hundred per cent, had to be the father of their suspect. On 30 December 2022 they went back and arrested Bryan Kohberger.
During his police interview, Kohberger refused to answer any questions
Delving into his background, they learned that he was a loner, known to be sociallyawkward and disconcerted people by staring at them with his big, bulging blue eyes.
He invaded their space and was not very good at talking to women.
His master’s degree in criminal justice in Pennsylvania was under the tutelage of an expert in serial killers. He then moved to Washington to pursue a PhD in criminology and justice and, as part of his studies, he had been a teaching assistant at WSU.
But this ended after growing complaints about his behaviour and conduct towards women.
“Many people came forward to say he was a strange individual and off-putting, who thought very highly of themselves. Almost narcistic,” says Anthony Dahlinger.
“He would be very demeaning to others based on his level of education versus theirs.
“He had a lot of interest in people who had committed heinous crimes – serial killers, and the like.
“We learnt that he bought the knife and sheath off Amazon a couple of months before he moved to Washington. According to his digital footprint and his mobile ping, he had been in or around the area of the King Road house 23 times before the killings. It was always late in the evening or early morning between 10pm and 4am.”
Police found a disturbing selfie on his phone after he had driven home from the murders and scrubbed himself in the shower. It shows him smiling and giving a thumbs up to the camera.
In Idaho, he was facing the death penalty. He maintained his innocence and his defence team did all they could to delay the case and try to get it kicked out. Then he took a plea deal.
He pleaded and agreed to waive his appeal rights in exchange for avoiding the death penalty.
Kohberger has never given any reason why he carried out such atrocious murders.
“No one knows why he did it or whether he even knew them,” says Anthony.
“He had been in the area of the house, circling it, from as early as July 2022.”
On 23 July, 2025, he was given four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole. He declined to make a statement himself and sat impassive during the victims’ family impact statements.
Looking across the courtroom at his daughter’s killer, Kaylee’s father, Steve
Goncalves, said, “In time, you will be forgotten to the wind. No visitors. Nothing more than initials on an unmarked tombstone.”
“Police officers tell us within minutes they had your DNA. Like a calling card. You were that careless. That foolish. That stupid masters degree? You’re a joke.”
Ben Mogen, Madison’s father, said she was much more than his only child.
“She was the only great thing I ever really did. And the only thing I was ever really proud of.”
He described struggling with addiction and substance abuse and how her daughter helped him.
“When I wasn’t wanting to live anymore, she was what would keep me from not caring.”
Scott Laramie, Madison’s stepfather, read a statement on behalf of him and her mother, Karen, saying their daughter was “Our gift of life, our purpose and our hope.”
Xana Kernodle’s stepfather, Randy Davis, told Kohberger, “You’re gonna go to hell … you’re evil … you took our children … you are gonna suffer, man.”

Bethany Funke wrote a statement, read aloud by a friend: “I hated and still hate that they are gone, but for some reason, I am still here, and I got to live,”
“Why did I get to live and not them? For the longest time, I could not even look at their families without feeling sick with guilt.”
An emotional Dylan Mortensen, was in court and read out her statement in person: “He didn’t just take their lives, he took the light they carried into every room. He took away the ability for me to tell them that I love them and that I’m so proud of them.”
